newsitem.title: PAKISTAN: Afghan factions focused on war, not negotiations.
newsitem.headline: Afghan factions focused on war, not negotiations.

text.p: Afghanistan's war seems set to intensify as the purist Islamic Taleban militia, reeling from the loss of the northern city of Mazar-i-Sharif, battles its foes on fronts north of Kabul, analysts said on Sunday.
"It would seem that the opposing sides want to fight it out," said Francis Okelo, senior political officer for the U.N. special envoy to Afghanistan, Norbert Holl.
"We are trying to say that's not the way to do it because at the end of the day it is not the military solution that will create peace in Afghanistan," he told Reuters.

The Taleban, most of whom are mainly ethnic Pashtun southerners, suffered a stinging reversal in the north last month, just as they seemed to have knocked out the main pillar in an anti-Taleban alliance, General Abdul Rashid Dostum.
On May 19, the Taleban forged a pact with General Abdul Malik, who then led a mutiny against Dostum, drove him into exile in Turkey and let Taleban fighters into Mazar-i-Sharif.

The pact swiftly fell apart amid friction between the Taleban and the northern capital's ethnic Uzbek and Shi'ite Moslem Hazara population. Malik's troops joined the opposition Shi'ite Hezb-i-Wahdat militia to expel the Taleban, who fled the city, leaving at least 300 dead and 700 prisoners.

While the Taleban were losing almost all their newly-gained territory in the north, opposition commander Ahmad Shah Masood broke out of his native Panjsher Valley to capture the strategic town of Jabal-os-Siraj at the foot of the Salang Pass.

See-saw fighting has raged around the town for the past nine days, but the Taleban have been unable to reopen the Salang highway that links Kabul to the north, where a Taleban force of up to 3,000 is stranded in Pul-i-Khumri, besieged by Malik's Uzbeks and an Ismaili militia that formerly held the town.

"Even if the Taleban retake Jabal-os-Siraj, the Salang Pass is a much tougher nut to crack," said a Western military analyst. "And it is questionable how long they can hold out in Pul-i-Khumri, which has no airport, without being resupplied."

The military setbacks have proved costly to the Taleban leadership. Their foreign minister, northern military chief and central bank governor are among Malik's captives, while the information and interior ministers are stuck in Pul-i-Khumri.
"This is very humiliating for them and their supporters," an Islamabad-based diplomat said. "The Taleban, overstretched and under stress, may be losing their mystique among the Pashtuns."
For now, the Taleban's defeat in the north seems to have sparked a burning desire for revenge rather than any willingness to negotiate with other ethnic, political and religious groups.
They have sought to prop up their position by rushing thousands of new recruits from Islamic religious schools in Pakistan across the border for a new onslaught on their foes.
"The Taleban seem intent on a new offensive, so we can expect a lot of fighting in the next few weeks and the split between north and south may intensify," the diplomat said.

He said opposition leaders, apart from Dostum, were stronger than before the May 19 Malik-Taleban deal, with the prestige of the Hezb-i-Wahdat militia led by Karim Khalili especially high after its role in the battle for Mazar-i-Sharif and its defence of the Hazara bastion of Bamiyan in central Afghanistan.
For Pakistan, widely seen as the Taleban's main foreign ally, the militia's change of fortunes has been a bitter blow.
Islamabad, which had withheld recognition of the Taleban government set up after the fall of Kabul in September, bestowed that accolade as soon as the Taleban entered Mazar-i-Sharif.

Pakistan, followed only by Saudi Arabia and the United Arab Emirates, informed its neighbours of its decision, but ignored the views -- ranging from suspicion to outright hostility -- of Iran, Russia and most Central Asian states.
"It's been an unmitigated diplomatic disaster for Pakistan," said the diplomat, who asked not to be identified.
Many Pakistani commentators agree.
"It is hard to believe Pakistan ever really thought its Afghan policy through," wrote columnist Aziz Siddiqui in Sunday's English-language Dawn newspaper.

"If it had, it couldn't have reasonably compromised on the need for a broad-based government of national reconciliation...It seems to have lost what leverage it could have exercised. It has agreed quietly to go where the Taleban lead it."
